State each assumption before the step that uses it.
A reader processes a derivation line by line,
and a condition that arrives after the line it governs
forces them to go back and reread that line with the condition in mind.
A first-time reader may not realize the line was incomplete,
and may conclude that the step is wrong or unjustified.

This covers every kind of condition:

- a restriction on a variable ("for $x \neq 2$");
- a hypothesis of a theorem;
- a case split;
- a fact that a step relies on.

Introduce the variable and its constraint together,
as in "let $x \neq 2$",
then write the steps that need the constraint.
When a step uses a fact proved earlier,
cite it in the justification on that line.

An assumptions list and a notation list are different lists:

- An assumptions list states conditions that the result depends on.
  Write it as a bullet list with "Suppose" or "Assume" once, before the list.
- A notation list names objects.
  Write it as a bullet list with "Let" or "Write" once, before the list.

End each lead-in with a colon,
and make each bullet complete the lead-in sentence.
Do not repeat the verb in every sentence,
and do not mix the two kinds of list in one list.
When both are needed, write the notation list first, because the assumptions use the names it introduces.

::: {#exm-assumptions-first}

## Stating the restriction on $x$ before using it

To show that $x = 2$ is a strict local minimizer of $f(x) = (x - 2)^2$,
we show that $f(x) > f(2)$ for every $x$ near 2 other than 2 itself.

> ❌
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> f(x) - f(2)
> &= (x - 2)^2 - 0 \\
> &> 0
> && \text{(for every } x \neq 2\text{)}
> \end{aligned}
> $$
>
> ✅ Let $x \neq 2$. Then
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> f(x) - f(2)
> &= (x - 2)^2 - 0
> && \text{(definition of } f\text{)}\\
> &> 0
> && \text{(} x - 2 \neq 0 \text{, so its square is positive)}
> \end{aligned}
> $$

In the ❌ version, the second line is false for $x = 2$,
and the reader learns this only from the note at its end.
In the ✅ version, "let $x \neq 2$" comes first,
so the reader reads each line already knowing which values of $x$ it covers,
and the justification says exactly where the condition is used.

:::

::: {#exm-assumptions-bullet-list}

## Writing several assumptions as one list

> ❌ Suppose $x \neq 2$.
> Suppose $f(x) = (x - 2)^2$.
> Suppose $x$ is less than $5$.
>
> ✅ Suppose:
>
> - $x \neq 2$,
> - $f(x) = (x - 2)^2$, and
> - $x$ is less than $5$.

The ✅ version writes "Suppose" once,
and the bullets show that the three assumptions are parallel and separate.

:::

::: {#exm-notation-bullet-list}

## Writing several names as one list

> ❌ Let $n$ be the sample size.
> Let $\bar{y}$ be the sample mean.
> Let $s$ be the sample standard deviation.
>
> ✅ Let:
>
> - $n$ be the sample size,
> - $\bar{y}$ be the sample mean, and
> - $s$ be the sample standard deviation.

These bullets name objects and assume nothing about them,
so this is a notation list.
If the result also needed a condition such as $n > 30$,
a separate assumptions list after this one would state it.

:::
